q.t: An axiom is a statement that is:
q.e: Axioms are the obvious starting truths; everything else is proved from them.

q.t: How many postulates did Euclid state?
q.e: Five postulates, specific to geometry, plus several general axioms (common notions).

q.t: According to Euclid, a point is that which has:
q.e: A point marks a position and has no size at all.

q.t: According to Euclid, a line is:
q.e: A line has length but no width or thickness.

q.t: Things which are equal to the same thing are:
q.e: If a = c and b = c, then a = b — Euclid’s first axiom.

q.t: According to Euclid, the whole is:
q.e: A part is only some of the whole, so the whole must be larger.

q.t: How many straight lines can be drawn through two distinct points?
q.e: Two points fix one and only one line.

q.t: A statement that has to be proved is called a:
q.e: Theorems are proved using axioms, postulates and earlier theorems.

q.t: According to Euclid, a surface has:
q.e: A surface is two-dimensional — no thickness.

q.t: Euclid’s famous book on geometry is called:
q.e: The Elements is in 13 books and organised geometry into definitions, axioms and proofs.

q.t: How many dimensions does a solid have?
q.e: Length, breadth and height.

q.t: How many dimensions does a surface have?
q.e: Length and breadth.

q.t: How many dimensions does a line have?
q.e: Length only.

q.t: How many dimensions does a point have?
q.e: It has position but no size.

q.t: The boundaries of a solid are:
q.e: Each step down loses a dimension: solids end in surfaces, surfaces in lines, lines in points.

q.t: ‘All right angles are equal to one another’ is one of Euclid’s:
q.e: It is his fourth postulate.

q.t: ‘A circle can be drawn with any centre and any radius’ is Euclid’s postulate number:
q.e: The third postulate — it is what a compass does.

q.t: ‘A terminated line can be produced indefinitely’ means that:
o: A line segment can be extended as far as we like
A line has two end points
q.e: This is the second postulate: a segment can always be made longer in a straight line.

q.t: If equals are added to equals, the wholes are:
q.e: If a = b, then a + c = b + c.

q.t: If AB = PQ and PQ = XY, then AB = XY. Which axiom is used?
o: Things equal to the same thing are equal to one another
The whole is greater than the part
q.e: Both AB and XY are equal to the same thing, PQ.

q.t: C lies between A and B on a line. Then AC + CB equals:
q.e: The two parts coincide exactly with the whole segment.

q.t: C is the midpoint of AB. Then AC equals:
q.e: AC = CB and AC + CB = AB, so 2AC = AB.

q.t: Euclid’s fifth postulate is about:
q.e: It says when two lines cut by a third must meet — equivalently, that there is only one parallel through a given point.

q.t: Two distinct lines cannot have more than how many points in common?
q.e: If they shared two points, both would be the single line through those points.

q.t: Playfair’s axiom states that through a point not on a line there is:
o: Exactly one line parallel to it
q.e: This is the modern, simpler form of Euclid’s fifth postulate.

q.t: If a = b, then a − c = b − c. Which axiom is this?
o: Equals subtracted from equals give equals
The whole is greater than the part
q.e: Taking the same amount from two equal things leaves equal remainders.

q.t: How many midpoints does a line segment have?
q.e: If there were two, each half would be both equal and unequal to the other — a contradiction.

q.t: A, B, C, D lie on a line in that order and AC = BD. Then:
q.e: Subtract the common part BC from both: AC − BC = BD − BC.

q.t: If AB = CD, then ½AB = ½CD. Which axiom is this?
o: The whole is greater than the part
q.e: Halving two equal things gives equal results.

q.t: By the fifth postulate, two lines cut by a transversal will meet on the side where the interior angles add up to:
q.e: On that side the lines lean towards each other. If the sum is exactly 180° they are parallel.

q.t: C is the midpoint of AB, AC = (3x − 1) cm and CB = (x + 5) cm. Find AB (in cm).
q.e: AC = CB: 3x − 1 = x + 5, so x = 3. AC = 8, AB = 16.

q.t: How many line segments are determined by 5 points on a line?
q.e: One for each pair of points: 5 × 4 ÷ 2.

q.t: A, B, C are on a line with AB = 5 cm, BC = 3 cm and AC = 8 cm. Which point is between the other two?
q.e: AB + BC = AC, so B lies between A and C.

q.t: Which of these is equivalent to Euclid’s fifth postulate?
o: Through a point outside a line there is exactly one parallel to it
A circle can be drawn with any radius
q.e: This is Playfair’s axiom; each can be proved from the other.

q.t: In Euclid’s system, the difference between axioms and postulates is that postulates:
q.e: Axioms (common notions) are used throughout mathematics; postulates are about geometric objects.

q.t: A system of axioms is called consistent when:
o: No contradiction can be deduced from it
Every statement in it is proved
q.e: If two axioms led to opposite conclusions, the whole system would be useless.

q.t: If x + y = 10 and x = z, then z + y = 10. This uses the idea that:
o: Equals may be substituted for equals
The whole is greater than the part
q.e: Since x and z are the same quantity, either can replace the other.

q.t: To construct an equilateral triangle on a segment AB, Euclid draws two circles with centres A and B and radius AB. Which postulate allows this?
o: The third — a circle with any centre and radius
The first — a line through two points
The fourth — right angles are equal
q.e: The circles meet at C with AC = AB = BC (radii), which gives the equilateral triangle.

q.t: P and Q are both midpoints of the same segment AB. What can we conclude?
o: P and Q are the same point
P and Q are 1 cm apart
q.e: AP = ½AB = AQ, so P and Q coincide — a segment has only one midpoint.

q.t: A, B, C lie on a line with B between A and C. AB = 2x, BC = x + 4 and AC = 25 cm. Find AB (in cm).
q.e: AB + BC = AC: 3x + 4 = 25, so x = 7 and AB = 14.
